title: Joel 2:18–27
context: The narrator reports the turning point: “Then the LORD was jealous for his land, and had pity on his people” (2:18). The LORD answers with promises: grain, wine, and oil; an end to reproach among the nations; and the removal of “the northern army” (2:19–20), which readers take as the locusts, a human invader, or both. The land, the animals, and the children of Zion are told not to fear but to rejoice, for the rains will return and the threshing floors will be full (2:21–24). Some translations and interpreters render “the early rain in just measure” (2:23) differently. The LORD promises to “restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten” (2:25), and twice says “my people will never again be disappointed” (2:26–27). In Hebrew numbering, this unit closes chapter 2, and 2:28–32 begins chapter 3. Shared ground: both traditions read the unit as God’s gracious answer to repentance and lament.

verses.text: Then the LORD was jealous for his land, and had pity on his people.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator reports that the LORD was jealous for his land and had pity on his people. Arminian readers see God responding to repentance with compassion, a real turn in the story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s pity as flowing from his covenant love, which also moved the people to seek him. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the turning point of the book; on God’s response, see the Judges 10:16 box.

verses.text: The LORD answered his people, “Behold, I will send you grain, new wine, and oil, and you will be satisfied with them; and I will no more make you a reproach among the nations.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD answers with grain, new wine, and oil, and promises no more reproach among the nations. Arminian readers see the specific losses of chapter 1 now reversed, answering the people’s lament.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s covenant blessings restored, compare Deuteronomy 7:13 by reference. Both traditions read the promise as God hearing the prayer of 2:17 and removing the reproach the priests feared.

verses.text: But I will remove the northern army far away from you, and will drive it into a barren and desolate land, its front into the eastern sea, and its back into the western sea; and its stench will come up, and its bad smell will rise.” Surely he has done great things.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will remove the northern army, driving it into desolate land and the seas. Arminian readers note that the northern army may be the locusts or a human enemy, and that readers hold both possibilities.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s power to remove whatever threat he has sent. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as deliverance from the destroyer, closing with the words surely he has done great things.

verses.text: Land, don’t be afraid. Be glad and rejoice, for the LORD has done great things.
verses.arminianNotes: Where the land mourned in 1:10, it now hears, Land, don’t be afraid. Arminian readers find in this direct address a tender reversal, as if the very soil were comforted by its Maker.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s great deeds as the ground of joy, compare Psalm 126:3 by reference. Both traditions read the address to the land as poetic and moving, showing the depth of the restoration.

verses.text: Don’t be afraid, you animals of the field; for the pastures of the wilderness spring up, for the tree bears its fruit. The fig tree and the vine yield their strength.
verses.arminianNotes: Even the beasts hear a word of comfort, as wilderness pastures sprout and fig and vine regain their strength. Arminian readers connect this with the panting animals of 1:20, whose cry has now been answered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers find here God’s care for every living thing, a theme sung in the psalms of creation. The promise to fig and vine, emblems of settled peace, signals that the curse of chapter 1 has been lifted.

verses.text: “Be glad then, you children of Zion, and rejoice in the LORD, your God; for he gives you the early rain in just measure, and he causes the rain to come down for you, the early rain and the latter rain, as before.
verses.arminianNotes: The children of Zion are to rejoice, for the LORD gives the early rain in just measure, and the latter rain as before. Arminian readers see the return of seasonal rains as God’s faithful provision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that some translations and interpreters render the phrase in just measure differently. Both traditions read the verse as joy in God’s gift of rain, and they hold the alternate renderings openly.

verses.text: The threshing floors will be full of wheat, and the vats will overflow with new wine and oil.
verses.arminianNotes: The threshing floors will be full of wheat, and vats will overflow with wine and oil. Arminian readers see abundance replacing scarcity, a concrete sign of God’s renewed favor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the overflowing vats as covenant blessing restored in full. Both traditions read the image as the reversal of 1:10 and 1:17, where grain, wine, oil, and granaries failed.

verses.text: I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten, the great locust, the grasshopper, and the caterpillar, my great army, which I sent among you.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will restore the years the locusts ate, my great army which I sent. Arminian readers see God’s restoring grace making up for what was lost, a deeply comforting promise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD names the locusts as his army, which he sent and now overrules. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as grace that redeems loss, and they handle its comfort pastorally.

verses.text: You will have plenty to eat and be satisfied, and will praise the name of the LORD, your God, who has dealt wondrously with you; and my people will never again be disappointed.
verses.arminianNotes: They will eat and be satisfied and praise the LORD who dealt wondrously, and his people will never again be disappointed. Arminian readers see gratitude and worship as the response to restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s wondrous dealings as the reason for praise and the guarantee of future hope. Both traditions read the closing promise as assurance for God’s people, while noting that its fullest sense is read in different ways.

verses.text: You will know that I am among Israel, and that I am the LORD, your God, and there is no one else; and my people will never again be disappointed.
verses.arminianNotes: They will know that the LORD is among Israel, that he is their God, and there is no other. Arminian readers see restored relationship as the goal, God dwelling with his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the exclusive claim, there is no one else, affirming the LORD’s unique deity. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the climax of the restoration, with the knowledge of God at its center.
